① Watch the Simulation
Dots are people; they grow larger and deeper blue as their capital grows. The spreading green glow marks where luck is passing and the red glow where bad luck is.
② Capital Distribution
The horizontal axis is final capital, the vertical axis is the number of people. Capital only doubles or halves, so only values of 10 × 2<sup>k</sup> appear.
③ Talent vs Final Capital
Each dot is one person. Higher talent doesn't put you higher up. The vertical axis is a log scale.
Richest
Most talented
④ How the Richest Person Got Rich
The gold line is the richest person's capital over time, the purple line is the most talented person's. Dots are the events they experienced.
Seized the luck
Luck came but missed
Bad luck
⑤ Results of 100 Repeats
What it shows: Even among people of similar talent, a few lucky breaks can open an extreme gap in wealth and success. It is very rare for the most successful person to be the most talented.

What it doesn't show: It doesn't mean talent is useless or effort is pointless. Real wealth is shaped by many factors such as education, inheritance and institutions; this model is a simplified one that keeps only luck and talent.
Original paper: Pluchino, Biondo, Rapisarda (2018), "Talent vs Luck: the role of randomness in success and failure"
The world is a 201×201 torus; events move 2 cells per step in a random direction, and an event counts as met when it comes within a radius of 1 cell.
The paper does not say what to do when several events are met in one step, so all of them are applied in the order met.
Running the default settings 300 times, the top 20% hold about 79% of capital (paper: 80%), and the richest person's median talent is about 0.67, only a little above the mean (0.6).
The code is available on GitHub.
How Do Stories Change as They're Retold? · Simulatio Lab
What survives and what disappears when a story is passed from person to person 40 times? Change memory and embellishment and try it yourself.
One person passes on a story they heard to the next, and that person passes it on again. When 12 chains starting from the same original are retold 40 times, what survives and what changes?

A story is a list of 30 motifs (events or details). Each motif hides a "how memorable is it" score (memorability), and the redder a block, the more memorable the motif. Some motifs are odd, unusual details.
When retelling, each teller recalls every motif with some probability. The more memorable the motif, the better it is recalled, and the higher the memory, the less is forgotten.

An odd detail is replaced with some probability (conventionality) by a plain, familiar motif; with some probability (embellishment) a new motif is invented and added; and occasionally two neighboring motifs swap places.
Twelve chains starting from the same original are passed on independently of each other. A solid outline marks a motif from the original story; a dashed outline marks one invented along the way.

① The Story Being Passed On

The top row is the original, and the 12 rows below are the stories the different chains are telling right now. Each box is one motif, and the redder it is, the more memorable. Boxes from the original have a bold outline.

② How Much of the Original Survives

The horizontal axis is the number of retellings, and the vertical axis is the share of the 30 original motifs still in the story. The bold blue line is the average of the 12 chains and the faint lines are the individual chains.
Average of the 12 chains
Each individual chain
③ The Remaining Story Becomes More Memorable
The red line is the average memorability of the motifs left in the story, and the gray dashed line is the original story's average. As the easily forgotten motifs drop out first, the average rises.
④ When Memory Changes

The horizontal axis is memory. Blue is the share of original motifs that remain, gold is how much the original motifs left in two different chains overlap (Jaccard similarity), and gray is an approximation of the overlap you would expect if the survivors were chosen by chance. Dots are 3 runs.
Original motifs remaining
Overlap between chains
Overlap expected by chance

What it shows: Stories do not wear down evenly as they are passed on. Plain details that are easy to forget disappear first and memorable details survive, so the average memorability of the remaining story goes up. Chains passed on independently also tend to keep the same motifs, so the overlap of the remaining motifs was higher than chance.

What it doesn't show: It does not mean human memory works like this model. It is a very simple toy model that lines motifs up in a row and keeps or removes them with probabilities; it does not capture the meaning of a story, its context, its audience or its wording. The distribution of "memorability" and "odd details", and the way new motifs are created, are all this project's assumptions.
